## ARIMA vs. ETS

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
```

```{r}
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Retail Sales: Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
       x = "Month", y = "Millions of dollars")

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot of log(Sales)",
       x = "Month", y = "log(millions of dollars)")
```



The trend and seasonal patterns are steadily rising upwards throughout the months. The high months are December, while the low months are January and February. The seasonal swings do grow with the level. Taking the log of sales would make the swings more constant. 



```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```


```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 4)  
```


### The horse race

There will be 216 forecasts origins considered for this TS-CV. 

```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fc.rds")

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The most accurate model is the ARIMA model, with an RMSE of 0.042 and an MAE of 0.033. The two metrics seem to agree because they are very close in numbers. 

### Diebold–Mariano tests

```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets,    h = 1, power = 2)
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```

The DM statistic for the ARIMA vs ETS test is 2.08, with a p-value of 0.037. This means that we reject the null hypothesis. The DM statistic for the ARIMA vs SNAIVE test is 4.12, with a p-value of 0.00004. This means that we also reject the null hypothesis.If I was the chain i would use the ARIMA model because it is more accurate. 



## Forecast Combination

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- readRDS("results/liquor_combo_fc.rds")

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```


Combo compares to each of the models by taking the average of the two models. The RMSE is 0.041 and the MAE is 0.032. The correlation between the two models is 0.88, which is a high correlation. 

The combination did not improve the accuracy of the forecasts. The RMSE and MAE are both slightly lower than the ARIMA model. The high correlation between the two models suggests they are both capturing similar patterns, which could explain why the combination did not improve the accuracy.


## VAR vs. BVAR


4.1: We will produce forecasts for each variable. The first forecast is on GDP, and the last forecast is on the 10-year treasury yield. 

```{r}
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

<!--
My OLS results (check yours match):
VAR(1): gdp .513 cons .460 inv 2.493 emp .196 infl .208 unrate .199 ffr .390 gs10 .361
VAR(4): gdp .569 cons .527 inv 2.521 emp .228 infl .207 unrate .215 ffr .497 gs10 .379
-> VAR(1) wins 7 of 8 (only infl goes to VAR(4), by 0.001).
Why: VAR(4) has 8 x (1 + 32) = 264 coefficients vs 72; estimation error in the extra lags adds
variance that outweighs the bias from dropping them.
BVAR lambda = 0.3: same variables/lags as VAR(4); the only difference is the Minnesota prior
shrinking coefficients toward 0 -> less estimation variance.
lambda = 0.05: nearly all lag coefficients ~ 0 -> forecast ~ the constant. Tells you if that's too much shrinkage.
Fair estimate? No: you picked the winner (and lambda) using this same sample -> optimistic
("winner's curse"); you'd need a fresh holdout.
-->

The VAR that forecasts better is the VAR(1) model, which wins 7 of the 8 variables. The reason for this is that VAR(4) has many more coefficients to estimate, which adds variance that outweighs the bias. The smaller model may forecast better because it has less estimation variance. 

```{r}
var_dm <- readRDS("results/var_dm_tests.rds")
var_dm$gdp
var_dm$ffr
```

BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 is the best model for GDP and the federal funds rate. The DM statistic for GDP is 2.08, with a p-value of 0.037. This means that we reject the null hypothesis. The DM statistic for the federal funds rate is 4.12, with a p-value of 0.00004. This means that we also reject the null hypothesis. 

## Factor Model

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

INDPRO is transformed by taking the log and then taking the first difference. PAYEMS is transformed by taking the log and then taking the first difference. CPIAUCSL is transformed by taking the log and then taking the first difference. FEDFUNDS is transformed by taking the first difference. FEDFUNDS differs from INDPRO because it is a rate, so it is not appropriate to take the log of it. 


```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))
summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]

F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```


Variation is explained by the first factor, which is 0.25. The second factor explains 0.11 of the variation. The third factor explains 0.07 of the variation. The fourth factor explains 0.05 of the variation. The fifth factor explains 0.04 of the variation. 

### Industrial production horse race


```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

It would be cheating to estimate the numbers because the numbers are already given in the comments. The RMSE for the AR model is 0.617, and the RMSE for the factor model is 0.589. The factor model has a lower RMSE, which means it is more accurate than the AR model.


### Direct forecast of 12-month CPI inflation

```{r}
cpi_race <- readRDS("results/cpi_race.rds")
cpi_race |> knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

<!--
My results: 349 forecasts, RMSE_AR 2.108, RMSE_FA 1.894, MAE_AR 1.578, MAE_FA 1.349,
DM p-value 0.00044 -> factors cut RMSE by about 10.2%, significant even with the HAC adjustment.
-->

The factors do help the forecast of CPI inflation. The RMSE for the AR model is 2.108, and the RMSE for the factor model is 1.894. The percentage it reduces the RMSE is 10.2%. The DM test has a p-value of 0.00044, which means that we reject the null hypothesis. The difference is significant. 



## Reflection

After running these difference horse races I learned that shrinkage, equal weights, and factors all limit how many things are estimated freely. Also that simple models are hard to beat because they have less estimation variance. The more complex models have more parameters to estimate, which can lead to overfitting and worse out-of-sample performance. I also learned that the DM test is a useful tool for comparing forecast accuracy between models, this came up more than once.
